authors: C. Kirabo Jackson; Rucker C. Johnson; Claudia Persico
title: The Effects of School Spending on Educational and Economic Outcomes: Evidence from School Finance Reforms *
key_finding: 12% increase in per-pupil school spending over 12 years → ~7% higher adult wages, higher HS completion, higher family income, lower adult poverty; effects strongest and most consistent for low-income children (school finance reform quasi-experiment).
effect_size_where: +12% pp spending → ~+7% adult wages (QUED — the landmark class)
design_class: quasi-experimental event-study/DiD (school finance reforms linked to PSID)
N: nationally representative cohorts born 1955-1985 linked to PSID
cost_per_unit_where: (spending increase modeled per-pupil, not per-unit program)

authors: Raj Chetty; John N. Friedman; Jonah E. Rockoff
title: Measuring the Impacts of Teachers I: Evaluating Bias in Teacher Value-Added Estimates
key_finding: Teacher value-added has within-school-year bias due to student sorting; across-school and multi-year estimates are far less biased — the bias problem is real but limited, not fatal.

title: Student Sorting and Bias in Value-Added Estimation: Selection on Observables and Unobservables
key_finding: Student sorting bias in VA estimation exists within school years but is largely absent across schools; supports the reliability of the teacher-effect signal across-school.
effect_size_where: (bias magnitude, not a causal program effect)

title: EDUCATION, WORK, AND CRIME: A HUMAN CAPITAL APPROACH*
key_finding: Human-capital model of crime where education raises opportunity cost of crime (foregone legitimate earnings + expected incarceration cost); predicts more-educated commit fewer crimes, with strongest effect on violent/property crimes.

title: The Effect of Education on Crime: Evidence from Prison Inmates, Arrests, and Self-Reports
key_finding: Additional years of schooling from compulsory-schooling reforms → significantly lower incarceration and arrest rates (esp. for black men); one additional year of schooling cuts imprisonment rates by the order of 0.3-0.4 pp for black males and ~0.1-0.2 pp for white males.
effect_size_where: 1 extra year schooling → ~0.3-0.4 pp lower imprisonment (black men), ~0.1-0.2 pp (white men)
design_class: quasi-experimental IV (compulsory schooling laws) + prison inmate, arrest, self-report data

authors: Brian Bell; Rui Costa; Stephen Machin
title: Crime, compulsory schooling laws and education
key_finding: UK compulsory schooling- Leaving Age reform: raising schooling reduces property crime (males) and vehicle crime; the effect operates via education's increased opportunity cost of crime.
effect_size_where: (UK RoSLA reform; property & vehicle crime reductions)

authors: James J. Heckman; Jora Stixrud; Sergio Urzua
title: The Effects of Cognitive and Noncognitive Abilities on Labor Market Outcomes and Social Behavior
key_finding: Cognitive and noncognitive skills jointly determine schooling, wages, occupation choice, and social behavior (crime, teen pregnancy, engagement in 'risky' social behavior); noncognitive skill is a distinct causal driver — human-capital policy should target both.

title: From Preschool to Adulthood: The Role of Child-Parent-Center Programs on Juvenile Arrest for Violent Offenses and Adult Income
key_finding: CPC preschool participation significantly lowers juvenile arrest for violent offenses, especially among higher-ACE subgroups; the effect partially mediates via reduced arrests on adult income (preschool → less violent crime → higher adult earnings).
effect_size_where: (see abstract: significant reduction in juvenile violent-crime arrest; mediation to income)
cost_per_unit_where: (n/a — CPC cost in prior Chicago studies ~$9-10k/child)

title: Intergenerational and Intragenerational Externalities of the Perry Preschool Project
key_finding: Perry Preschool treatment effects extend to the treated participants' own children: fewer school suspensions, higher education/employment, less crime in children of untreated vs. treated; effects largest for children of male participants.
effect_size_where: (intergenerational transmission, no headline effect size in abstract)

authors: Joshua D. Angrist; Alan B. Krueger
title: Does Compulsory School Attendance Affect Schooling and Earnings?
key_finding: Compulsory attendance laws bind for a subset of students; IV around quarter-of-birth shows a genuine causal effect of schooling on earnings for that margin — establishing the causal baseline for education→earnings.
effect_size_where: small but positive causal schooling-on-earnings effect at the compulsory marginal

authors: Stephen J. Machin; Olivier Marie; Suncica Vujic
title: The Crime Reducing Effect of Education
key_finding: Compulsory-school-leaving-age reform in England & Wales → significant property-crime reduction (RD design on school-leaving age law); education improvement is a causal crime-reduction lever.
effect_size_where: significant drop in property crime off the reform
N: England & Wales cohorts subject to school-leaving-age change

authors: Raj Chetty; John N. Friedman; Jonah E. Rockoff
title: Measuring the Impacts of Teachers II: Teacher Value-Added and Student Outcomes in Adulthood
key_finding: High-VA teachers → higher college attendance, higher adult salaries, lower teen pregnancy; replacing a bottom-5% VA teacher with an average one raises classroom lifetime income ~$250k.
effect_size_where: +$250,000 present-value lifetime income per classroom (bottom-5% → average teacher swap)
design_class: quasi-experimental (teacher VA linked to tax records)
N: 1.0-1.2 million students (~2.5M in Chetty-Friedman-Rockoff combined studies)
